scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Vessels of the Ancestors: The Power of Kumina

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Kumina emerged through the practices of indentured labourers and enslaved people brought to Jamaica from the Kongo region of central Africa.
In the second half of the 19th century, it syncretised with Myalism and distinguished itself from Zion Revivalism by rejecting the Bible as the central authority behind worship.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ceremonies are primarily linked to healing sick individuals through singing, dancing, drumming, animal sacrifice, and spirit possession.
Participants seek to receive knowledge and prophecies from ancestral spirits.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment centres on the main kbandu drum, supported by shakas, scrapes, and catta sticks.
Songs incorporate Kikongo terms and serve to communicate with the ancestral world.
Listen for the kbandu, shakas, râpes, bâtons catta.
Drumming driven by the principal kbandu drum, accompanied by shakas, scrapes, and catta sticks, supporting call-and-response singing with Kikongo terms that accelerates through the night.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Imogene 'Queenie' Kennedy, known as Queenie III (c.1920–1998), was a renowned Kumina Queen born in St. Thomas who later lived in Kingston and Waterloo, St. Catherine.
Primarily associated with St. Thomas in eastern Jamaica, the practice also spread to Portland, St. Mary, St. Catherine, and the city of Kingston.
Syncretised with Myalism in the 19th century and influenced Rastafari drumming (Nyabinghi) as well as modern dancehall and reggae.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Kumina is a sacred religious healing tradition involving spirit possession and ancestor veneration; outsiders must respect ritual boundaries and avoid treating sacred ceremonies as secular entertainment.
